statement: In US adults followed for up to about four years in the national PATH cohort, and in three reviews commissioned by governments, the evidence is insufficient to say whether vaping, compared with using neither cigarettes nor e-cigarettes, changes the risk of heart disease, stroke or long-term lung disease, and the sources read give no cancer rates for people who vape; this is not evidence that vaping has no effect. The cohort found no detectable difference in newly reported heart disease or stroke between people who only vaped and people who used neither, with wide intervals and few events, and a higher rate of newly reported lung conditions in people who had used e-cigarettes, which smoking history may explain. Heart (Berlowitz et al., 2022, a research letter; PATH Waves 1 to 5, 2013–2019; funded by the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, the Food and Drug Administration's Center for Tobacco Products and the American Lung Association; one author reports grants from Johnson & Johnson): of 24,027 adults with no heart disease at the start, 1,487 reported a new diagnosis of heart disease or stroke over up to four years: 764 of 14,832 who used neither product, 41 of 822 who only vaped, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both (counts, not rates: the groups differ in age and follow-up; the age-adjusted rates as printed were, in that order, 8.0, 9.7, 14.8 and 17.1 per 1,000 person-years, which the editors could not reproduce from the counts). After adjustment for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, body mass index, blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, family history, marijuana use, pack-years and other tobacco, the hazard ratio against using neither was 1.00 (95% CI 0.69–1.45) for people who only vaped, 1.53 (1.30–1.79) for people who only smoked and 1.54 (1.21–1.96) for people who did both; for heart attack, heart failure or stroke alone (15 events among people who only vaped) 1.35 (0.75–2.42), 2.20 (1.73–2.81) and 2.08 (1.40–3.09). Against people who only smoked the ratio was 0.66 (0.46–0.94) for people who only vaped (0.61, 0.34–1.09, for the narrower outcome) and 1.01 (0.81–1.26) for people who did both (0.94, 0.65–1.36). The outcomes were self-reported and not adjudicated; the comparison group included people who had stopped smoking; and people who only vaped had more pack-years than that group (mean 11.0 against 4.2, with spreads several times the means), so past smoking may account for part of a difference or hide one. Lungs (Xie et al., 2020; PATH Waves 1 to 4, 2013–2018; same funders; one author reports grants from Ethicon, a Johnson & Johnson subsidiary, and other authors report federal grants and, for one, personal fees from several pharmaceutical companies): of 21,618 adults with no respiratory condition at the start, 1,460 (6.8%) reported a new diagnosis of asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis. After adjustment for age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, region, smoking history (never; former by years since quitting; current by pack-years), other tobacco, other drug use, body mass index and chronic conditions, the adjusted rate was 26.06 against 20.41 per 1,000 person-years (about 2.6 against 2.0 in 100 a year, editors' conversion) in people who had ever used e-cigarettes at the start against people who had not (rate ratio 1.28, 1.10–1.48), with the same ratio for former use (1.28), which includes people who had tried 1 or 2 puffs, and a similar one for current use (1.31, 1.08–1.59); by condition, COPD 1.62, emphysema 1.54, chronic bronchitis 1.33 and asthma 1.24 (1.01–1.53). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone the ratios were much larger (2.14 for any condition, 5.03 for COPD), which shows how much depends on handling past smoking; use was recorded at the first wave only; 401 people (16.0% of those currently vaping) had never smoked cigarettes, so most had smoked; and the ratio was 1.20 (0.99–1.45) among people with no chronic condition at the start. Residual confounding by how much people smoked and when they stopped is likely, and the authors say causality cannot be established. The reviews. The National Academies (2018; contract with the Food and Drug Administration; its Reviewers page lists one reviewer employed by British American Tobacco Research and Development Centre; its online table of study sponsors was not read) found no available evidence whether e-cigarette use is associated with coronary heart disease, stroke or peripheral artery disease, none whether e-cigarettes cause respiratory disease, none on intermediate cancer endpoints and none on long-term illness or death in people who both vape and smoke; it judged the evidence substantial for a short-term rise in heart rate and moderate for a rise in diastolic blood pressure after nicotine intake, moderate for more cough and wheeze, and for an association with more asthma attacks, in adolescents who vape (four cross-sectional, self-reported studies), limited for better lung function or fewer COPD flare-ups in adults with asthma or COPD who switched from smoking (small studies), and substantial for fewer short-term adverse health outcomes in several organ systems when people switched completely from smoking (mostly small studies). The UK review (2022; commissioned by the Office for Health Improvement and Disparities; search to July 2021; no declarations of interest on the pages read) said that, as in 2018, there is still no available evidence on clinical cardiovascular outcomes and that the extent of cardiovascular risk remains uncertain, rated the evidence from lung tests insufficient either way and limited for fewer COPD flare-ups in adults who switch completely (two reports on one group of patients), and presented no cancer incidence data; the review questions it lists concern markers linked to risk and people with existing conditions, so the pages read do not show a search for new disease in the general population (editors' reading; the Methods are in a PDF not read). The Australian review (Banks et al., 2023; Department of Health and the National Health and Medical Research Council; no relevant disclosures; searches to July 2020, with major reviews to December 2021) rated clinical cardiovascular outcomes and invasive cancer as no available evidence and asthma, bronchitis and COPD as insufficient evidence in people who smoke and no available evidence in people who do not, with certainty low or very low, and judged the direct effect on clinical disease largely unknown; it also judged it conclusive that vaping products cause an acute lung injury (EVALI), largely with THC-containing products, though in the largest study 14% of cases reported only nicotine products. The heart analysis appeared after all three reviews' searches ended; the lung analysis appeared after the Australian top-up search and neither is named in the Australian paper's reference list or on the UK pages read; a published critique of the Australian review (Mendelsohn et al., 2022, Drug and Alcohol Review) was not read. Not known: whether vaping causes any heart disease, lung disease or cancer in people who have never smoked, over more than four years or with current devices; whether the higher rate of lung conditions reflects vaping or past smoking; and cancer rates. Certainty: very low. Status: single study (two analyses of one cohort, which share data and some authors and are not independent replications).
plain: In two analyses of one large US study (more than 20,000 adults followed for up to four years), people who only vaped did not have a clearly different rate of new heart disease or stroke from people who used no cigarettes or e-cigarettes (hazard ratio 1.00, range 0.69 to 1.45, from only 41 cases), while people who smoked, or smoked and vaped, had about 1.5 times the rate. The same study found more new lung conditions such as COPD and asthma in people who had used e-cigarettes (about 2.6 against 2.0 in 100 people a year), but most of them had smoked, and allowing fully for past smoking is hard. Three reviews commissioned by governments, whose searches ended before the heart analysis was published, found no evidence or too little evidence on heart attack, stroke, long-term lung disease or cancer from vaping, so no one can yet say whether vaping causes them. A lung injury outbreak (EVALI) was linked to vaping products, mostly ones containing THC. The studies are short, rest on what people reported and cannot show cause.
population: US adults in the national PATH cohort followed from 2013–2014 for up to about four years: 24,027 with no heart disease or stroke at the start (heart analysis, Waves 1 to 5) and 21,618 with no asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis at the start (lung analysis, Waves 1 to 4); most of the people who vaped had smoked (in the lung analysis 16.0% of those currently vaping had never smoked cigarettes); and the reviews of the wider literature by the National Academies (2018), the UK government (2022; search to July 2021) and the Australian government (2023; studies to July 2020, major reviews to December 2021)
exposure: Vaping (e-cigarette use): current use of any frequency, updated at each wave (heart analysis), or ever, former or current use at the first wave only (lung analysis), with or without smoking
comparator: People who used neither cigarettes nor e-cigarettes (the heart analysis's reference group, which includes people who had stopped smoking); people who only smoked cigarettes; people who both vaped and smoked; in the lung analysis, people who had never used an e-cigarette (including people who smoked)
outcome: Newly reported, self-reported diagnoses of heart disease or stroke (heart analysis) and of asthma, COPD, emphysema or chronic bronchitis (lung analysis) over up to about four years; and what three reviews concluded about heart disease, lung disease and cancer
magnitude: Absolute counts and rates before ratios. Heart (Berlowitz et al., 2022; PATH Waves 1 to 5; 24,027 adults with no heart disease at the start; up to 4 years): new self-reported diagnosis of heart disease or stroke in 764 of 14,832 people who used neither product, 41 of 822 who only vaped, 569 of 6,515 who only smoked and 113 of 1,858 who did both (counts only; the groups differ in age and follow-up); age-adjusted rates as printed per 1,000 person-years 8.0, 9.7, 14.8 and 17.1 in that order (not reproducible from the counts). Hazard ratios against using neither, fully adjusted: only vaping 1.00 (0.69–1.45), only smoking 1.53 (1.30–1.79), both 1.54 (1.21–1.96); for heart attack, heart failure or stroke (519 cases, 15 among people who only vaped) 1.35 (0.75–2.42), 2.20 (1.73–2.81) and 2.08 (1.40–3.09). Against people who only smoked: only vaping 0.66 (0.46–0.94) and 0.61 (0.34–1.09); both 1.01 (0.81–1.26) and 0.94 (0.65–1.36). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone, only vaping against neither 1.16 (0.82–1.66) and 1.55 (0.87–2.76). Lungs (Xie et al., 2020; PATH Waves 1 to 4; 21,618 adults with no respiratory condition at the start; up to about 4 years): 1,460 (6.8%) with at least one new diagnosis (asthma 804, emphysema 336, COPD 573, chronic bronchitis 948 new diagnoses); adjusted rate per 1,000 person-years for any condition: never used 20.41 (18.65–22.17), ever 26.06 (22.63–29.49), former 26.12, current 26.68 (21.83–31.52) (about 2.0 against 2.6–2.7 in 100 a year, editors' conversion); for single conditions, never against ever: COPD 6.48 against 10.49, emphysema 3.74 against 5.76, chronic bronchitis 12.18 against 16.23, asthma 10.73 against 13.31. Rate ratios against never use (fully adjusted, ever / former / current): any condition 1.28 (1.10–1.48) / 1.28 (1.09–1.51) / 1.31 (1.08–1.59); chronic bronchitis 1.33 / 1.31 / 1.33; emphysema 1.54 / 1.42 / 1.69; COPD 1.62 / 1.66 / 1.57; asthma 1.24 (1.01–1.53) / 1.19 (0.95–1.50) / 1.32 (1.01–1.72). Adjusted for age, sex and race/ethnicity alone the ratios for ever use were 2.14 (any condition), 4.02 (emphysema) and 5.03 (COPD). Among people with good or better self-rated health (18,649): former 1.21 (1.00–1.47), current 1.43 (1.14–1.80); among people with no chronic condition at baseline (14,865): ever 1.20 (0.99–1.45), former 1.11 (0.90–1.37), current 1.40 (1.09–1.79). Reviews (the authors' own gradings): National Academies 2018 conclusions 9-1 (clinical cardiovascular outcomes, no available evidence), 11-1 (respiratory disease, no available evidence), 10-1 (intermediate cancer endpoints, no available evidence), 18-3 (long-term illness or death in people who vape and smoke, no available evidence), 11-4 (cough and wheeze in adolescents, moderate), 11-2 and 11-3 (adults with asthma or COPD who switch, limited); UK review 2022: clinical cardiovascular outcomes still no available evidence, cardiovascular risk uncertain, lung tests insufficient, no cancer incidence data; Australian review 2023: clinical cardiovascular outcomes and invasive cancer no available evidence, asthma, bronchitis and COPD insufficient in people who smoke and no available evidence in people who do not, certainty low or very low, EVALI conclusive (14% of cases in the largest study reported only nicotine products, 2% only non-nicotine products). Follow-up: up to 4 years in both cohort analyses; the reviews' evidence mostly concerns short-term effects.

evidence.extracted: Exposure was recorded at the first wave only; former use means ever use, even 1 or 2 puffs, and not now; current use means every day or some days; retention 83.2% (Wave 2), 78.4% (Wave 3), 73.5% (Wave 4). Outcomes were self-reported physician diagnoses in the past 12 months. Authors' stated limits: self-reported exposure and diagnoses; observational data with relatively short follow-up, so causality could not be established; no time-varying exposure or confounding; device characteristics unavailable; lung function not measured. They also describe reverse causation (people with early symptoms switching to e-cigarettes or quitting) as a bias that could hide an association.

evidence.extracted: Chapter 11 (cardiovascular): as in 2018, to date there is still no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with clinical cardiovascular outcomes (coronary heart disease, stroke, peripheral arterial disease) or subclinical atherosclerosis. Overall, the extent to which vaping presents a risk for cardiovascular health remains uncertain, though the authors expect the risk to be much less than that of cigarette smoking based on the toxicant profile. 27 of the 41 included studies were cross-over or acute-exposure designs that cannot answer questions about cardiovascular health outcomes; the authors call for studies comparing rates of coronary heart disease, peripheral arterial disease and stroke between people who use no nicotine, people who use tobacco and people who vape. No study was found in people with an existing cardiovascular condition. Animal studies (16) suggest possible long-term changes; no human evidence.

evidence.extracted: Chapter 10 (respiratory; 25 studies, no meta-analyses): the authors conclude there is insufficient evidence from spirometry, exhaled nitric oxide, impulse oscillometry, bronchoscopy and imaging on whether vaping affects lung function after acute, short-to-medium or long-term exposure; imaging and bronchoscopy studies were very short-term or confounded by tobacco or cannabis smoking in the vaping groups. Asthma (4 small studies): limited evidence that vaping negatively affects lung function among adults with asthma, and differences in designs, diagnoses and measurements prevent any conclusions. COPD: two articles from the same group of patients reported improvements in some spirometry measures in the group that used vaping products compared with baseline and none in the group that smoked; the authors conclude limited evidence for fewer exacerbations in adults who smoke, have COPD and switch completely, for up to 5 years. Cell and animal studies (47 in vitro, 25 animal): aerosol may cause airway adverse effects in these models. The authors say studies of long-term vaping are urgently needed and that it is not clear whether the spirometry changes are large enough to matter clinically.

evidence.extracted: Chapter 9 (cancer): the National Academies found no available evidence on whether vaping is associated with cancer risk and the Committee on Toxicity found existing evidence insufficient; this review calls the human literature growing but still modest. Biomarkers of exposure to several carcinogens are lower in people who vape than in people who smoke (the authors call this conclusive evidence of lower exposure); inflammation and oxidative stress findings show no systematic relationship and are insufficient to draw conclusions; gene expression and DNA methylation studies (8, none from the UK) are limited by missing smoking comparison groups; no study assessed people with an existing or previous cancer; cell and animal studies are hard to translate. The authors state that biomarker studies need longer follow-up to show whether vaping reduces cancer risk compared with smoking. No cancer incidence data are presented.

evidence.extracted: Scope and cut-off (Chapters 2, 7, 11 and 16): the authors conducted two systematic reviews (health risks of vaping; harm perceptions); for the health chapters they first summarised the 2018 Public Health England review, the National Academies 2018 report and the Committee on Toxicity report, then their own review, using an algorithm to decide on meta-analyses (Table 6 of Chapter 2 of the full report, not seen). The search cut-off for the health chapters was July 2021, and the authors note that new studies have since been published and recommend continual updating. evidence.extracted: Certainty (Results › Health outcomes, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph): rated low or very low for clinical and subclinical outcomes, because of small samples, study design and a paucity of evidence that caused serious concerns about inconsistency, imprecision and indirectness; the authors conclude the direct impact of e-cigarettes on clinical disease outcomes is largely unknown. Discussion › Limitations: people who have never smoked are the most reliable group in which to estimate effects of e-cigarettes, people who neither smoke nor use e-cigarettes should be the main comparison group, adjustment is unlikely to fully remove confounding between e-cigarette use and smoking, and comparisons with smoking do not permit reliable ascertainment of the direct health impact of e-cigarettes.

risk_of_bias.note: Both cohort analyses are rated high on ROBINS-E (cards sc_berlowitz_2022 and sc_xie_2020): residual confounding by smoking history, since most people who vaped had smoked, the heart analysis's reference group includes people who had stopped smoking and the group that only vaped had more pack-years (mean 11.0 against 4.2, spreads several times the means); self-reported, non-adjudicated diagnoses; exposure recorded at the first wave only in the lung analysis. The three reviews are provisional or critically low on AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_nasem_2018, sc_banks_2023, sc_mcneill_2022). Counted once.

inconsistency.note: The two analyses answer different questions (heart and lung) and do not conflict; the three reviews agree that clinical outcomes have not been studied, and the cohort results do not contradict them.

indirectness.note: Direct for the claim as worded (newly reported diagnoses in adults over up to four years, and what reviews found). The wording does not reach cancer, people who have never smoked, longer use or current devices, and says so.

imprecision.note: Only 41 (any heart disease or stroke) and 15 (heart attack, heart failure or stroke) events occurred among people who only vaped, so the hazard ratios 1.00 (0.69–1.45) and 1.35 (0.75–2.42) fit a lower rate, no change or a clearly higher rate; the intervals for single lung conditions are wide (for example asthma, current use 1.32, 1.01–1.72).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable. Both cohort analyses use data from one federally funded study and declare no tobacco or vape industry funding; the reviews are reported as they state their own evidence.

large_effect.note: The lung ratios (about 1.2 to 1.7) are modest and fell sharply when smoking history was added; the heart ratio for people who only vaped is 1.00. No upgrade.

dose_response.note: Exploratory highest rates with every-day use, first use before age 25 and established use (values in a supplement not read); not counted.

plausible_confounding.note: Residual confounding by smoking more plausibly raises the lung ratios, while reverse causation (people with early symptoms switching to vaping) could hide an association; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational cohorts start low. Downgraded once for risk of bias (both analyses rated high on ROBINS-E) and once for imprecision (few events in people who only vaped), which reaches the floor, very low. Rated as worded: the claim is that the evidence is insufficient to say whether vaping changes the risk of heart or lung disease, not that vaping has no effect; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. The three reviews' judgments (no available evidence, insufficient evidence, low or very low certainty) are their authors' judgments and are reported, not adopted. Overlap: the heart and lung analyses are two analyses of one cohort that share data and some authors, so they are not independent replications; the reviews overlap in the studies they draw on. The acute lung injury outbreak (EVALI) is outside the rating: the Australian review judged it conclusive, largely with THC-containing products. Funding is set out in the statement: no tobacco or vape industry funding is declared for the cohort analyses or the reviews read; the pharmaceutical and device-company ties of some authors are listed as printed, and the sponsors of the studies in the National Academies report are in an online table that was not read.
